the following questions: (a) How do Chinese perceive their relative social status and how does it relate to their health outcomes, after a wide range of socioeconomic characteristics are taken into account?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relative status hypothesis has gained increasing empirical support.
the relationship between perceived social status and health is complex and depends on the level of perceived social status.
the study of subjective social status and social mobility in China has been a relatively neglected area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results of this study are consistent with the relative status hypothesis, which posits that people in the lower rungs in a social hierarchy have worse health because of the gap between their circumstances and those of others (Wilkinson 1996).
we are interested in the relationship between social status, social mobility and health outcomes.
the study of social status and health has emphasized the effects of perceived relative status on health above and beyond objective social characteristics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the health effects of subjective social status are largely due to the effects of subjective status mobility, and that the latter is a stronger predictor of health than the former.
the health effects of subjective social position in a society with rapid economic development and social change are not simply a reflection of the effects of objective economic inequality.
the health effects of relative social status are not only affected by one’s current status, but also by the changes in one’s social position over time.
